newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Israeli-Syrian talks a matter of time - Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Israeli-Syrian talks a matter of time - Mubarak.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Sunday that a fresh start to peace talks between Israel and Syria was just a question of time and could take place at any moment.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speaking to reporters after his first meeting with Mubarak since July, said the United States was working on a formula for new talks with Syria, which broke down almost a year ago.
"We're discussing the formula to achieve resumption of the talks. The Americans are doing this and I hope they'll be successful," Netanyahu said.
Mubarak, asked for his views on the chances for Syrian-Israeli talks, said: "The prospects for starting the talks are possible at any time.
"I believe Syria says it's ready to start the talks, even if it may have some reservations. But this is question of time and it's bound to be resolved."

In a news conference earlier the Egyptian president linked progress on the Syrian-Israeli track to faithful Israeli implementation of its latest agreements with the Palestinians, including last month's deal on the West Bank town of Hebron.

"I think good faith in implementing the Hebron agreement, then go through with negotiations on the final status (of Jerusalem), this will remove the suspicion which is existing" between Israel and the Syrians and Lebanese, he said.

Negotiations "on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks must be resumed without delay" on the basis of the principle of land for peace, added Mubarak, who played a key intermediary role in achieving the Hebron accord.

Syria has not taken the Hebron agreement as a sign of a change of heart by Netanyahu's right-wing government, which took power in June. Damascus says talks must resume where they left off and that Israel had given a private commitment to withdraw from all of the Golan Heights.
On their troubled bilateral relationship, Mubarak and Netanyahu both renewed their commitment to cooperate for the sake of a wider Middle East peace.

"I had a very good meeting with President Mubarak. We talked about advancing peace on all fronts...about advancing our bilateral relations, including in the economic field, and we are committed to doing that," Netanyahu said.
""Egypt and Israel are the cornerstone of peace in the Middle East and we are going to pursue on that foundation peace with everyone," he added.

Mubarak, who for months refused to meet Netanyahu until Israel agreed with the Palestinians on Hebron, said: :It was a very good meeting and I hope we can continue like this and enhance the peace process."
Netanyahu later held talks with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, who is also attending the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in the Swiss resort of Davos.
Arafat has brought a list of complaints about Israeli delays in carrying out some aspects of old peace agreements and Mubarak told his news conference that Arafat was pessimistic.
Mubarak, who acts as unofficial sponsor of the Palestinian negotiating team, urged Israel to keep to its agreements.
"Policies and practices which are illegal and inconsistent with the spirit of peace, such as settlement activities, should be avoided and stopped altogether," Mubarak added.

Mubarak said it was important to get progress towards opening an airport and a seaport in Gaza, under control of Arafat's Palestinian Authority, and implement other parts of overall accords on peace in the region.
Such moves were essential for the welfare of ordinary Palestinians. "Otherwise they will revolt against their regime," said Mubarak, speaking in English.

Any people would rise up against a leader who was not seen to be doing all he could for them, he added in an echo of concerns voiced by other officials in the region that Israeli intransigence could feed radical opposition to Arafat.
